question: Find the names of the four members of the US women's 3X3 basketball team at the 2020 Olympics. Find out what their final college team was and who the head coach of their final college team was during the 2022/2023 season, as well as the name of the team player with the highest average points per game for that season and the team player with the highest average rebounds per game for that season. Provide a bulleted list with the name of the 3X3 team member, the name of their final college, the name of the coach in the 2022/2023 season, the name of the team player with the highest average points in the 2022/2023 season, and the name of the team player with the highest average rebounds in the 2022/2023 season in a comma separated list for each bullet point. Order the bullet list in alphabetical order by the player's first name. Do not list any other information.

# USA Basketball 3x3 at the Olympics
3x3 basketball was featured as an Olympic sport for the first time at the 2020 Tokyo Games (held in 2021). The United States are the only team to medal in multiple Games and made history as the first Olympic 3x3 women’s gold medal winner with a team featuring WNBA players Stefanie Dolson, Allisha Gray, Kelsey Plum and Jackie Young.

## Roster Named for USA Basketball Women’s 3x3 Olympic Qualifying Team
Mon, Feb 17, 2020, 9:34 PM
/
USA Basketball
The four-member rosters today were announced for the USA Basketball Men’s and Women’s 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournament Teams that will compete in the 2020 FIBA 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournament March 18-22 in Bengaluru, India, where the top three finishing men’s and women’s teams will earn berths into the 2020 Tokyo Olympic Games.
Named to the USA women’s team were current WNBA players: Napheesa Collier (Minnesota Lynx/O’Fallon, Mo.), Stefanie Dolson (Chicago Sky/Port Jervis, N.Y.), Allisha Gray (Dallas Wings/Sandersville, Ga.) and Kelsey Plum (Las Vegas Aces/Poway, Calif.).
The rosters were selected by the USA Basketball 3×3 Selection Committees following Feb. 12-15 training camps in Chicago that featured 11 female and 16 male hopefuls.
“USA Basketball is grateful to all of the athletes who attended training camp and competed for a roster spot,” said Jay Demings, USA Basketball Youth & Sport Development director and member of the USA Basketball 3×3 Men’s and Women’s Selection Committees. “It was a very talented field for both the men and women, and the committees had a very difficult task in selecting these teams. In the end, we are confident in the abilities of the eight players and the strength of the teams overall. Now, it is on to the very important task of qualifying the USA for the 3×3 Olympic basketball competition in Tokyo.”
The USA women earned their spot in the FIBA 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournament by virtue of their status on the FIBA 3×3 world rankings as of this past November.
As per FIBA regulations, all teams taking part in the 2020 FIBA 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournament must include on their rosters at least two athletes who are ranked among the federation’s top 10 FIBA 3×3 athletes.
On the women’s side Collier, Dolson and Plum also are members of the 2020 USA Basketball Women’s National Team and have won gold medals with USA Basketball.

## Roster Named for USA Basketball Women’s 3x3 Olympic Qualifying Team
Additionally, Collier won gold at the 2014 Youth Olympic Games, which is a 3×3 competition.
The 2020 Olympics for the first time will feature the inclusion of 3×3 basketball with eight men’s and eight women’s teams competing for gold July 25-29 in Tokyo.
On the women’s side, Russia, China, Mongolia and Romania earned Olympic bids by virtue of their top FIBA 3×3 world rankings.
Twenty men’s and 20 women’s teams will compete for three Olympic qualifying berths in the March 18-22 FIBA 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournaments.
The USA women at the FIBA 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournament will play in Group A with France, Germany, Uruguay and Indonesia. Group B includes Iran, Japan, Ukraine, Turkmenistan and Australia. Group C features Netherlands, Estonia, Belarus, Hungary and Sri Lanka. And, in Group D will be Italy, Taipei, Switzerland, Spain and host India.
The eighth and final Olympic 3×3 spots will be awarded based on FIBA’s universality clause, which is designed to offer an Olympic 3×3 berth to one country in the men’s and the women’s tournament who did not have a team at the 2012 or 2016 Olympic basketball tournaments. The FIBA Universality Qualifying Tournaments, which will be held in April 2020 in Budapest Hungary, will include six men’s and six women’s teams. The top men’s and women’s finishers will advance to the Olympics.
An exciting and fast-paced game, 3×3 officially was unveiled in international competition at the 2010 Youth Olympic Games and since has become a fan favorite at FIBA 3×3 World Cup events. Played on a half court with a 10-minute clock, and a 12-second shot clock, the first team to 21 points, or the team in the lead at the end of regulation, is the winner.
The USA Basketball 3×3 Women’s Selection Committee includes: Demings, Carol Callan(USA Basketball Women’s National Team director) and Kareem Maddox.

## Roster Named for USA Basketball Women’s 3x3 Olympic Qualifying Team
Mon, Feb 17, 2020, 9:34 PM
/
USA Basketball
The four-member rosters today were announced for the USA Basketball Men’s and Women’s 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournament Teams that will compete in the 2020 FIBA 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournament March 18-22 in Bengaluru, India, where the top three finishing men’s and women’s teams will earn berths into the 2020 Tokyo Olympic Games.
Named to the USA women’s team were current WNBA players: Napheesa Collier (Minnesota Lynx/O’Fallon, Mo.), Stefanie Dolson (Chicago Sky/Port Jervis, N.Y.), Allisha Gray (Dallas Wings/Sandersville, Ga.) and Kelsey Plum (Las Vegas Aces/Poway, Calif.).
The rosters were selected by the USA Basketball 3×3 Selection Committees following Feb. 12-15 training camps in Chicago that featured 11 female and 16 male hopefuls.
“USA Basketball is grateful to all of the athletes who attended training camp and competed for a roster spot,” said Jay Demings, USA Basketball Youth & Sport Development director and member of the USA Basketball 3×3 Men’s and Women’s Selection Committees. “It was a very talented field for both the men and women, and the committees had a very difficult task in selecting these teams. In the end, we are confident in the abilities of the eight players and the strength of the teams overall. Now, it is on to the very important task of qualifying the USA for the 3×3 Olympic basketball competition in Tokyo.”
The USA women earned their spot in the FIBA 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournament by virtue of their status on the FIBA 3×3 world rankings as of this past November.
As per FIBA regulations, all teams taking part in the 2020 FIBA 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournament must include on their rosters at least two athletes who are ranked among the federation’s top 10 FIBA 3×3 athletes.
On the women’s side Collier, Dolson and Plum also are members of the 2020 USA Basketball Women’s National Team and have won gold medals with USA Basketball.
texts.3:
## Roster Named for USA Basketball Women’s 3x3 Olympic Qualifying Team
Additionally, Collier won gold at the 2014 Youth Olympic Games, which is a 3×3 competition.
The 2020 Olympics for the first time will feature the inclusion of 3×3 basketball with eight men’s and eight women’s teams competing for gold July 25-29 in Tokyo.
On the women’s side, Russia, China, Mongolia and Romania earned Olympic bids by virtue of their top FIBA 3×3 world rankings.
Twenty men’s and 20 women’s teams will compete for three Olympic qualifying berths in the March 18-22 FIBA 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournaments.
The USA women at the FIBA 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournament will play in Group A with France, Germany, Uruguay and Indonesia. Group B includes Iran, Japan, Ukraine, Turkmenistan and Australia. Group C features Netherlands, Estonia, Belarus, Hungary and Sri Lanka. And, in Group D will be Italy, Taipei, Switzerland, Spain and host India.
The eighth and final Olympic 3×3 spots will be awarded based on FIBA’s universality clause, which is designed to offer an Olympic 3×3 berth to one country in the men’s and the women’s tournament who did not have a team at the 2012 or 2016 Olympic basketball tournaments. The FIBA Universality Qualifying Tournaments, which will be held in April 2020 in Budapest Hungary, will include six men’s and six women’s teams. The top men’s and women’s finishers will advance to the Olympics.
An exciting and fast-paced game, 3×3 officially was unveiled in international competition at the 2010 Youth Olympic Games and since has become a fan favorite at FIBA 3×3 World Cup events. Played on a half court with a 10-minute clock, and a 12-second shot clock, the first team to 21 points, or the team in the lead at the end of regulation, is the winner.
The USA Basketball 3×3 Women’s Selection Committee includes: Demings, Carol Callan(USA Basketball Women’s National Team director) and Kareem Maddox.

## Roster Named for USA Basketball Women’s 3x3 Olympic Qualifying Team
Mon, Feb 17, 2020, 9:34 PM
/
USA Basketball
The four-member rosters today were announced for the USA Basketball Men’s and Women’s 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournament Teams that will compete in the 2020 FIBA 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournament March 18-22 in Bengaluru, India, where the top three finishing men’s and women’s teams will earn berths into the 2020 Tokyo Olympic Games.
Named to the USA women’s team were current WNBA players: Napheesa Collier (Minnesota Lynx/O’Fallon, Mo.), Stefanie Dolson (Chicago Sky/Port Jervis, N.Y.), Allisha Gray (Dallas Wings/Sandersville, Ga.) and Kelsey Plum (Las Vegas Aces/Poway, Calif.).
The rosters were selected by the USA Basketball 3×3 Selection Committees following Feb. 12-15 training camps in Chicago that featured 11 female and 16 male hopefuls.
“USA Basketball is grateful to all of the athletes who attended training camp and competed for a roster spot,” said Jay Demings, USA Basketball Youth & Sport Development director and member of the USA Basketball 3×3 Men’s and Women’s Selection Committees. “It was a very talented field for both the men and women, and the committees had a very difficult task in selecting these teams. In the end, we are confident in the abilities of the eight players and the strength of the teams overall. Now, it is on to the very important task of qualifying the USA for the 3×3 Olympic basketball competition in Tokyo.”
The USA women earned their spot in the FIBA 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournament by virtue of their status on the FIBA 3×3 world rankings as of this past November.
As per FIBA regulations, all teams taking part in the 2020 FIBA 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournament must include on their rosters at least two athletes who are ranked among the federation’s top 10 FIBA 3×3 athletes.
On the women’s side Collier, Dolson and Plum also are members of the 2020 USA Basketball Women’s National Team and have won gold medals with USA Basketball.

## Roster Named for USA Basketball Women’s 3x3 Olympic Qualifying Team
Additionally, Collier won gold at the 2014 Youth Olympic Games, which is a 3×3 competition.
The 2020 Olympics for the first time will feature the inclusion of 3×3 basketball with eight men’s and eight women’s teams competing for gold July 25-29 in Tokyo.
On the women’s side, Russia, China, Mongolia and Romania earned Olympic bids by virtue of their top FIBA 3×3 world rankings.
Twenty men’s and 20 women’s teams will compete for three Olympic qualifying berths in the March 18-22 FIBA 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournaments.
The USA women at the FIBA 3×3 Olympic Qualifying Tournament will play in Group A with France, Germany, Uruguay and Indonesia. Group B includes Iran, Japan, Ukraine, Turkmenistan and Australia. Group C features Netherlands, Estonia, Belarus, Hungary and Sri Lanka. And, in Group D will be Italy, Taipei, Switzerland, Spain and host India.
The eighth and final Olympic 3×3 spots will be awarded based on FIBA’s universality clause, which is designed to offer an Olympic 3×3 berth to one country in the men’s and the women’s tournament who did not have a team at the 2012 or 2016 Olympic basketball tournaments. The FIBA Universality Qualifying Tournaments, which will be held in April 2020 in Budapest Hungary, will include six men’s and six women’s teams. The top men’s and women’s finishers will advance to the Olympics.
An exciting and fast-paced game, 3×3 officially was unveiled in international competition at the 2010 Youth Olympic Games and since has become a fan favorite at FIBA 3×3 World Cup events. Played on a half court with a 10-minute clock, and a 12-second shot clock, the first team to 21 points, or the team in the lead at the end of regulation, is the winner.
The USA Basketball 3×3 Women’s Selection Committee includes: Demings, Carol Callan(USA Basketball Women’s National Team director) and Kareem Maddox.

Bio
Tina Langley has established herself as one of women’s college basketball’s premier program builders, earning a national reputation for transforming multiple programs into thriving championship contenders. A proven coach with multiple Final Four appearances and a track record of on- and off-the-court success, Langley has twice inherited teams near the bottom of their conferences and elevated them into nationally ranked programs. At Washington, she has restored the Huskies to recent national prominence, guiding the program to consecutive NCAA Tournament appearances and reestablishing its place among the nation’s Top 25.
Named the 12th head coach in Washington history on April 5, 2021, Langley enters the 2026–27 season after engineering one of the nation’s most impressive turnarounds. Since arriving on Montlake, she has led steady year-over-year progress, taking the Huskies from last place in the Pac-12 to a No. 24 final Associated Press ranking and the highest NET finish in program history at No. 22 in 2026. In just five seasons, she has transformed Washington into a consistent postseason contender with national momentum. Langley’s teams are known for their discipline, offensive efficiency and defensive toughness.
The foundation of that resurgence was laid quickly and has correlated with Langley’s relentless commitment to a values-based, people-first culture. Nothing speaks to this more prominently than the Huskies’ unprecedented continuity across their entire basketball operation.

# Tina Langley - Women's Basketball
In 2022–23, Washington improved from seven wins to 19, marking the second-largest single-season turnaround in program history. In Washington’s inaugural Big Ten season (2024–25), the Huskies also made history by leading the conference in field goal percentage (49.5%), three-point percentage (40.1%) and free throw percentage (83.6%) during league play while finishing the regular season on a five-game winning streak. The Huskies have since reached the NCAA Tournament in back-to-back seasons for the first time in more than a decade, highlighted by a No. 6 seed in 2026.
During the 2025–26 campaign, Washington recorded 22 victories, 10 conference wins, seven road wins and 13 home wins, all the program’s highest totals since 2016–17. The 2025–26 Huskies also earned a school-record six victories over Top 30 NET opponents and built one of the nation’s elite defenses, holding eight NCAA Tournament teams to their lowest or second-lowest scoring outputs of the season.
Player acquisition and development have also been a hallmark of Langley’s career and is demonstrated in the multiple individual awards her players have received. In 2025–26, Sayvia Sellers earned First Team All-Big Ten honors, Avery Howell received All-Big Ten Honorable Mention recognition, and Brynn McGaughy was selected to the unanimous All-Big Ten Freshman Team. Across her coaching career, Langley has developed 56 all-conference performers in total and coached 14 WNBA Draft selections. At Washington, Dalayah Daniels became the program’s first WNBA Draft pick since 2017, while Elle Ladine and Nancy Mulkey also advanced to the professional ranks under her leadership.

# Tina Langley - Women's Basketball
During her first three seasons at Washington, Langley secured three consecutive top 15 recruiting classes, including four five-star prospects. By 2026, she signed five McDonald’s All-Americans, more than the program had secured in all previous years combined. She has also prioritized roster continuity, with Washington becoming one of only three Division I programs to avoid losing a player to the transfer portal following the 2024–25 season and one of just two Power 4 programs to return three all-conference players on the same roster the following year.
Off the court, Langley has fostered a culture centered on academic achievement and holistic student-athlete development. Under her leadership, Washington’s team GPA increased to 3.46, the program posted a perfect NCAA Academic Progress Rate for four consecutive years, and 19 student-athletes earned conference All-Academic recognition.
Prior to Washington, Langley orchestrated another transformational rebuild at Rice, leading the Owls through the most successful period in program history. Rice compiled a 44–4 conference record from 2018–21, captured three consecutive Conference USA championships, won the 2021 WNIT title and earned the program’s first Associated Press Top 25 ranking. She was named Conference USA Coach of the Year in 2019.
Langley also thrived as an assistant in multiple roles at Maryland, including five as associate head coach. She helped guide the Terrapins to consecutive Final Four appearances in 2014 and 2015, multiple conference championships and several of the nation’s top recruiting classes.
Before Maryland, Langley served on the staffs at Georgia (2005), Clemson (2003–05) and Toledo (1998–03), where she advanced from graduate assistant to associate head coach.
A former collegiate student-athlete at Bevill State and West Alabama, Langley earned her bachelor’s degree in special education from West Alabama and later completed a master’s degree in counseling.

Bio
Tina Langley has established herself as one of women’s college basketball’s premier program builders, earning a national reputation for transforming multiple programs into thriving championship contenders. A proven coach with multiple Final Four appearances and a track record of on- and off-the-court success, Langley has twice inherited teams near the bottom of their conferences and elevated them into nationally ranked programs. At Washington, she has restored the Huskies to recent national prominence, guiding the program to consecutive NCAA Tournament appearances and reestablishing its place among the nation’s Top 25.
Named the 12th head coach in Washington history on April 5, 2021, Langley enters the 2026–27 season after engineering one of the nation’s most impressive turnarounds. Since arriving on Montlake, she has led steady year-over-year progress, taking the Huskies from last place in the Pac-12 to a No. 24 final Associated Press ranking and the highest NET finish in program history at No. 22 in 2026. In just five seasons, she has transformed Washington into a consistent postseason contender with national momentum. Langley’s teams are known for their discipline, offensive efficiency and defensive toughness.
The foundation of that resurgence was laid quickly and has correlated with Langley’s relentless commitment to a values-based, people-first culture. Nothing speaks to this more prominently than the Huskies’ unprecedented continuity across their entire basketball operation.

# Tina Langley - Women's Basketball
In 2022–23, Washington improved from seven wins to 19, marking the second-largest single-season turnaround in program history. In Washington’s inaugural Big Ten season (2024–25), the Huskies also made history by leading the conference in field goal percentage (49.5%), three-point percentage (40.1%) and free throw percentage (83.6%) during league play while finishing the regular season on a five-game winning streak. The Huskies have since reached the NCAA Tournament in back-to-back seasons for the first time in more than a decade, highlighted by a No. 6 seed in 2026.
During the 2025–26 campaign, Washington recorded 22 victories, 10 conference wins, seven road wins and 13 home wins, all the program’s highest totals since 2016–17. The 2025–26 Huskies also earned a school-record six victories over Top 30 NET opponents and built one of the nation’s elite defenses, holding eight NCAA Tournament teams to their lowest or second-lowest scoring outputs of the season.
Player acquisition and development have also been a hallmark of Langley’s career and is demonstrated in the multiple individual awards her players have received. In 2025–26, Sayvia Sellers earned First Team All-Big Ten honors, Avery Howell received All-Big Ten Honorable Mention recognition, and Brynn McGaughy was selected to the unanimous All-Big Ten Freshman Team. Across her coaching career, Langley has developed 56 all-conference performers in total and coached 14 WNBA Draft selections. At Washington, Dalayah Daniels became the program’s first WNBA Draft pick since 2017, while Elle Ladine and Nancy Mulkey also advanced to the professional ranks under her leadership.
texts.6:
# Tina Langley - Women's Basketball
During her first three seasons at Washington, Langley secured three consecutive top 15 recruiting classes, including four five-star prospects. By 2026, she signed five McDonald’s All-Americans, more than the program had secured in all previous years combined. She has also prioritized roster continuity, with Washington becoming one of only three Division I programs to avoid losing a player to the transfer portal following the 2024–25 season and one of just two Power 4 programs to return three all-conference players on the same roster the following year.
Off the court, Langley has fostered a culture centered on academic achievement and holistic student-athlete development. Under her leadership, Washington’s team GPA increased to 3.46, the program posted a perfect NCAA Academic Progress Rate for four consecutive years, and 19 student-athletes earned conference All-Academic recognition.
Prior to Washington, Langley orchestrated another transformational rebuild at Rice, leading the Owls through the most successful period in program history. Rice compiled a 44–4 conference record from 2018–21, captured three consecutive Conference USA championships, won the 2021 WNIT title and earned the program’s first Associated Press Top 25 ranking. She was named Conference USA Coach of the Year in 2019.
Langley also thrived as an assistant in multiple roles at Maryland, including five as associate head coach. She helped guide the Terrapins to consecutive Final Four appearances in 2014 and 2015, multiple conference championships and several of the nation’s top recruiting classes.
Before Maryland, Langley served on the staffs at Georgia (2005), Clemson (2003–05) and Toledo (1998–03), where she advanced from graduate assistant to associate head coach.
A former collegiate student-athlete at Bevill State and West Alabama, Langley earned her bachelor’s degree in special education from West Alabama and later completed a master’s degree in counseling.

Bio
Tina Langley has established herself as one of women’s college basketball’s premier program builders, earning a national reputation for transforming multiple programs into thriving championship contenders. A proven coach with multiple Final Four appearances and a track record of on- and off-the-court success, Langley has twice inherited teams near the bottom of their conferences and elevated them into nationally ranked programs. At Washington, she has restored the Huskies to recent national prominence, guiding the program to consecutive NCAA Tournament appearances and reestablishing its place among the nation’s Top 25.
Named the 12th head coach in Washington history on April 5, 2021, Langley enters the 2026–27 season after engineering one of the nation’s most impressive turnarounds. Since arriving on Montlake, she has led steady year-over-year progress, taking the Huskies from last place in the Pac-12 to a No. 24 final Associated Press ranking and the highest NET finish in program history at No. 22 in 2026. In just five seasons, she has transformed Washington into a consistent postseason contender with national momentum. Langley’s teams are known for their discipline, offensive efficiency and defensive toughness.
The foundation of that resurgence was laid quickly and has correlated with Langley’s relentless commitment to a values-based, people-first culture. Nothing speaks to this more prominently than the Huskies’ unprecedented continuity across their entire basketball operation.

# Tina Langley - Women's Basketball
In 2022–23, Washington improved from seven wins to 19, marking the second-largest single-season turnaround in program history. In Washington’s inaugural Big Ten season (2024–25), the Huskies also made history by leading the conference in field goal percentage (49.5%), three-point percentage (40.1%) and free throw percentage (83.6%) during league play while finishing the regular season on a five-game winning streak. The Huskies have since reached the NCAA Tournament in back-to-back seasons for the first time in more than a decade, highlighted by a No. 6 seed in 2026.
During the 2025–26 campaign, Washington recorded 22 victories, 10 conference wins, seven road wins and 13 home wins, all the program’s highest totals since 2016–17. The 2025–26 Huskies also earned a school-record six victories over Top 30 NET opponents and built one of the nation’s elite defenses, holding eight NCAA Tournament teams to their lowest or second-lowest scoring outputs of the season.
Player acquisition and development have also been a hallmark of Langley’s career and is demonstrated in the multiple individual awards her players have received. In 2025–26, Sayvia Sellers earned First Team All-Big Ten honors, Avery Howell received All-Big Ten Honorable Mention recognition, and Brynn McGaughy was selected to the unanimous All-Big Ten Freshman Team. Across her coaching career, Langley has developed 56 all-conference performers in total and coached 14 WNBA Draft selections. At Washington, Dalayah Daniels became the program’s first WNBA Draft pick since 2017, while Elle Ladine and Nancy Mulkey also advanced to the professional ranks under her leadership.

# Tina Langley - Women's Basketball
During her first three seasons at Washington, Langley secured three consecutive top 15 recruiting classes, including four five-star prospects. By 2026, she signed five McDonald’s All-Americans, more than the program had secured in all previous years combined. She has also prioritized roster continuity, with Washington becoming one of only three Division I programs to avoid losing a player to the transfer portal following the 2024–25 season and one of just two Power 4 programs to return three all-conference players on the same roster the following year.
Off the court, Langley has fostered a culture centered on academic achievement and holistic student-athlete development. Under her leadership, Washington’s team GPA increased to 3.46, the program posted a perfect NCAA Academic Progress Rate for four consecutive years, and 19 student-athletes earned conference All-Academic recognition.
Prior to Washington, Langley orchestrated another transformational rebuild at Rice, leading the Owls through the most successful period in program history. Rice compiled a 44–4 conference record from 2018–21, captured three consecutive Conference USA championships, won the 2021 WNIT title and earned the program’s first Associated Press Top 25 ranking. She was named Conference USA Coach of the Year in 2019.
Langley also thrived as an assistant in multiple roles at Maryland, including five as associate head coach. She helped guide the Terrapins to consecutive Final Four appearances in 2014 and 2015, multiple conference championships and several of the nation’s top recruiting classes.
Before Maryland, Langley served on the staffs at Georgia (2005), Clemson (2003–05) and Toledo (1998–03), where she advanced from graduate assistant to associate head coach.
A former collegiate student-athlete at Bevill State and West Alabama, Langley earned her bachelor’s degree in special education from West Alabama and later completed a master’s degree in counseling.

### A star is born
“He just allows me to play free, and allows me to spread my wings and just play my game,” Gray said of Smesko. “I feel like I’ve always been that player. It’s just that sometimes, you gotta find the right fit. And me coming to Atlanta was like that fit for me, where I was really able to take over and really score it.”
It meant a lot to Smesko to have a veteran like Gray believe in him and his vision from Day 1.
“I think it’s really important that players believe in what you’re doing if you want to get anything accomplished. Because I don’t care how good your ideas are, it is the players who execute them, and they’re going to make it work,” Smesko explained. “Lish was one of the people that was willing to try anything right away. We do things a little differently, and we have a different language, and they’ve been in the league a long time. They could have taken it a different way, but they were excited about it, and they wanted to give it a go.”
The team broke records. Gray was elevated to the top of the opposition’s scouting report. She was getting more interview requests last year from local and national media than she did in her previous eight seasons in the league combined.
She was a household name.
But then, the playoffs began, and the Dream lost to the Indiana Fever in three games despite the Fever being without Caitlin Clark for the entire series.
Gray finished in the top four in MVP voting and was selected to the All-WNBA first team, but the loss still left a sour taste in her mouth.
“I never want to experience that feeling again,” Gray said, in reflection.

### Bring in the reinforcements
Remember the trade that brought her to Atlanta? Well, it wasn’t just the organization that wanted her here – and to be clear, they 100 percent did – but it was also at the behest of one specific person: Rhyne Howard.
“I found out that Rhy actually requested me, so that made it even more cool for me,” Gray said.
The two – along with Naz Hillmon, who was part of the foundation of the Dream from 2022 – have become inseparable.
They are professionals, yes, but they are also best friends off the court.
Gray and Howard can often be found on the golf course during days off – those look a little bit different now due to the growing eyes on the team – as well as filming several food reviews and other TikToks together.
After that loss to Indiana last year in the playoffs, Howard went to the front office and asked them to get them more help to make a championship run with this squad.
They listened.
“Being here and being a part of the group that set the foundation, we didn’t want to continue to feel like the franchise was nothing,” Howard said during the team’s season-opening press conference. “We didn’t want it to feel like what we came into. Basketball is what we do to make our money and business, but you still need the support around you to feel supported and have fun and what we are doing.”
And like with Lish, Howard had a specific player in mind to join the team: Angel Reese.
“If Rhy sends for you, you better get in the car and come,” Gray said. “When she sends for you in that car, you better get in that car because she ain’t circling the block for you again.”
The team pushed their chips all-in with the acquisition of Reese, trading multiple first-round picks for her.
She’s more than lived up to the expectations, breaking the single-season rebound record and single-game rebound record, while elevating her offense and defense.
This is where she wanted to be, too.
She wanted to be in Atlanta, but she wanted to be with Gray and Howard.

### Bring in the reinforcements
“They’re great vets,” Reese told The IX Sports. “Outside of the basketball stuff, they always are making sure that I’m good. Like they’re the first people to check on me with anything that’s going on. Basketball-wise, you don’t have to do it once the game is done, they don’t have to talk, because this is a business, honestly. But they genuinely care about me and the sisterhood in the locker room has been amazing. It’s something that I really needed, so I’m really grateful for them.”
And while they are teaching Reese how to win – she’ll be making her first playoff appearance in her three-year career with Atlanta – she’s teaching Gray how to be what she is off of the court.
A superstar.
“I was telling Lish that you’re a superstar, and she doesn’t realize that all the time. When we go places, they want to meet certain people,” Reese told The IX Sports. “She loves T.I., so I’m like, ‘You’re a superstar.’ Like, you go through the back entrance, you don’t go through the front.
“I’m trying to show her that you’re a star. All of those chants are for you, because you’re a superstar, and you belong here.”
It’s something that Gray has taken time to adjust to – even with that All-Star performance a couple of years ago.
“I guess it’s just like that humble nature of me. But yeah, Angel like she reiterates over and over that, ‘I _am_ Atlanta. There are no rules. We are Atlanta. We are superstars, and we need to start acting like it.’
“I’m like, you know what? Yeah, you’re right. I am a superstar. Like I do need to take advantage of my perks.”
That came to fruition during Atlanta’s Birthday Bash in May, when she got to see T.I. in concert.
When asked about her favorite song, Gray said, “Big Things Poppin’,” which was fitting for the play of the Dream this year.
Gray even got to meet The Rubber Band Man after the show.
A superstar, indeed.

### Quiet no longer
After each game, win or lose, the Dream huddle in front of their bench. Hillmon traditionally addressed the group first, serving as Atlanta’s vocal leader.
That’s not a role that Gray takes on, but that doesn’t mean that she is the quiet person that everyone thinks she is.
Take, for instance, an in-arena, mid-timeout video package that played in Gateway Center Arena.
Over the beat of Glorilla’s “WHATCHU KNO ABOUT ME,” Gray and Howard were rapping the lines to Dr. Suess’ Green Eggs and Ham over the beat.
Players like Jones, Paopao, and Indya Nivar had to cover their mouths to stifle their laughter.
It’s an example of the personality that sometimes shines through from Gray, despite the quiet, shy demeanor.
When asked about her quiet demeanor, Staley interrupted the question.
“She’s not quiet anymore,” she said, with a laugh. “She’s incredibly funny.”
And she’s not afraid to be the butt of the joke, either. During a video series called “Rewind the Tape,” I asked Gray to go over her high school scouting report.
In the report, it said that she had “springs in her legs” for her ability to jump.
She made a joke about needing some WD-40 for her knees now.
Likewise, during the team’s first preseason game, there was a Spanish player on the Dream’s training camp roster named Maite Cazorla.
During a pre-game media session, Gray was asked if she could speak Spanish or would learn how to from her teammate.
She said, “Me llamo Lish. Adios,” before ending the interview with a laugh.
Despite claiming that she doesn’t block shots, Gray blocks a fair number, especially for a guard.
But for her, she denies it and says, “That’s not me. That’s AI.”

### Big brand Lish
“I can’t tell you. I cannot tell you,” Wilson told The IX Sports in June when trying to get her to spill the news about a potential PE coming for her friend. “That’s her news to break for if she is, or if she’s not, but I can’t tell you that. But it’s definitely something special. And I always beam with so much more when she wears my shoes because she doesn’t have to, but she chooses to, and I’m glad that she likes it.”
It also doesn’t hurt that the league signed a new CBA, which allowed players to be paid fairly.
Last year, during the final season of the previous CBA, Gray made $190,000. After the new agreement was reached, when the overwhelming majority of players were free agents, Gray inked a new deal worth $1,190,000 in 2026 that increases over the next two seasons.
“It’s so crazy because like you’re young and you just remember like being in the backyard playing, and then you get to high school, and then you get to college, and then you get to the pros, and it’s just like I just sit back and I’ll be like, I be like, ‘wow, I made it,’” Gray reflected.
“Then, with the new CBA money, I’m like, ‘whoa, I really made it,’ because then it’s just like it allows me to throw a couple extra bucks to my parents and get them nice things that I wasn’t able to do in the past. So it’s just like I wake up looking at that bank account, and you know, just being able to realize that, wow. Like, I did it! I really made it!”
The added attention isn’t always positive attention. It’s been that way throughout the league over the last few years. With the added eyeballs comes the added trolls.
It isn’t new to Gray.
That mural in her hometown? It was vandalized in 2022 with racist comments written on it by three men.
“I just give my energy to the people who deserve it. I give my energy to people that also reciprocate that same energy back to me,” she said. “I’m not gonna waste my time on negative people and bad thoughts because that can take a toll on your mental health, as well.

### Big brand Lish
“So I think for me, I’m good at reading a person. Before I intrude on somebody or talk to them, I kind of like to sit back and study you and see how you move and how you talk to people. Are you nice? Are you respectful? And then from there, after my first conversation with you, I know that like, ‘OK, this is somebody that I can continue to talk to, or like, no, this is a one-time conversation for me, because for me, like I’ve always told, first impressions mean a lot. My spirit is too positive and fun to be wasted on negative people.”

## Still one goal to achieve
During the All-Star break this year, Gray joined her fellow All-Stars at the Barack Obama Presidential Center for a practice before the game.
The namesake came out and introduced himself to players and took photos – including with Gray.
Allisha Gray standing with Barack Obama (Photo credit: Allisha Gray on Threads)
Add that to the list of big-time moments for her to achieve this year, along with meeting T.I. and even having the rapper personalize a message for her during her Goggle Lish game.
“I was so happy. That made my night,” Gray told reporters after the game. “I took a picture with Obama, a picture with T.I, and got a personal message video from T.I. Year made.”
But there is one more thing that could make her year even better.
Despite all of the hardware. Despite being a multi-millionaire from playing the game that she has loved since she was playing in the backyard as a kid, Gray still has more to accomplish.
She didn’t say win the MVP, though she wouldn’t mind it.
She didn’t say lead the league in scoring (“the S in SG stands for shooting,” she said).
No.
The one goal that she wants to accomplish has nothing to do with her. It has to do with her team.
“The W Championship. That’s literally like the only thing from my career that is missing is a W Championship, and I feel like that’s something everybody wants to win,” Gray explained. “I really do feel like we have the team to accomplish that goal. We just gotta really lock in and stick to the game plan and really hone down on like the little minor mistakes that we tend to make. But I truly believe that we have the team to accomplish that goal this season.”
Even if that doesn’t happen this year, the team is confident in the players they have and the vision that they have for the future.
And that future, no matter what, includes Gray.
Something that her friends and family are proud of.
“With Lish, I think she’s happy in Atlanta. They allowed her to grow up,” Staley said. “She has a handful of friends who are super competitive and allowed her to grow. They are rising together at the top of their games.”

## Still one goal to achieve
“I’m glad that she’s seeing pieces surrounding her to be able to help her drive and continue to drive,” Wilson added. “But, I think she feels really good in Atlanta. I’m just glad that she’s found a home for herself. Because it shouldn’t be like, ‘no, I’m stable here,’ but it should be ‘I’m trying to make my footprint here.’ That’s what Lish is doing.”
And as far as her family goes, they couldn’t be happier to have her nearby.
“Having her come to Atlanta has been a blessing for us as a family, for her as a player,” Allen Gray said. “The class and the way that this organization is run is somewhere that she feels at home. She wants to end her career here because of the support and the wraparound services that they offer here in Atlanta. All of her needs are met, all of her requests are met, and the way that they take care of our daughter, we really appreciate it.”
So, all that leaves is Gray.
Just a kid from Sandersville. A quiet kid who loves the outdoors. Loves her family, her friends, her people.
She’s as close to her hometown as she can be, but in Atlanta, she _is_ home.
And that is where she wants to stay.
“I’m loved here in Atlanta. Atlanta has made me like this organization has made me feel so great about myself,” she said. “That’s why when it was time to extend and re-sign, there was no hesitation for me. This is a place I definitely want to retire and finish my career, playing for the Dream.
“It’s just the support here is so amazing. The little kids really like to make me feel good because no matter how I play, I can have an on night, off night; they don’t see that. All they see me as is Allisha the person, and they make me feel good regardless of the game that I have.”

Title: Just a kid from Sandersville: Becoming Allisha Gray
Chunks: 11,12,13,14,18,19,20,21
### A star is born
“He just allows me to play free, and allows me to spread my wings and just play my game,” Gray said of Smesko. “I feel like I’ve always been that player. It’s just that sometimes, you gotta find the right fit. And me coming to Atlanta was like that fit for me, where I was really able to take over and really score it.”
It meant a lot to Smesko to have a veteran like Gray believe in him and his vision from Day 1.
“I think it’s really important that players believe in what you’re doing if you want to get anything accomplished. Because I don’t care how good your ideas are, it is the players who execute them, and they’re going to make it work,” Smesko explained. “Lish was one of the people that was willing to try anything right away. We do things a little differently, and we have a different language, and they’ve been in the league a long time. They could have taken it a different way, but they were excited about it, and they wanted to give it a go.”
The team broke records. Gray was elevated to the top of the opposition’s scouting report. She was getting more interview requests last year from local and national media than she did in her previous eight seasons in the league combined.
She was a household name.
But then, the playoffs began, and the Dream lost to the Indiana Fever in three games despite the Fever being without Caitlin Clark for the entire series.
Gray finished in the top four in MVP voting and was selected to the All-WNBA first team, but the loss still left a sour taste in her mouth.
“I never want to experience that feeling again,” Gray said, in reflection.

### Bring in the reinforcements
Remember the trade that brought her to Atlanta? Well, it wasn’t just the organization that wanted her here – and to be clear, they 100 percent did – but it was also at the behest of one specific person: Rhyne Howard.
“I found out that Rhy actually requested me, so that made it even more cool for me,” Gray said.
The two – along with Naz Hillmon, who was part of the foundation of the Dream from 2022 – have become inseparable.
They are professionals, yes, but they are also best friends off the court.
Gray and Howard can often be found on the golf course during days off – those look a little bit different now due to the growing eyes on the team – as well as filming several food reviews and other TikToks together.
After that loss to Indiana last year in the playoffs, Howard went to the front office and asked them to get them more help to make a championship run with this squad.
They listened.
“Being here and being a part of the group that set the foundation, we didn’t want to continue to feel like the franchise was nothing,” Howard said during the team’s season-opening press conference. “We didn’t want it to feel like what we came into. Basketball is what we do to make our money and business, but you still need the support around you to feel supported and have fun and what we are doing.”
And like with Lish, Howard had a specific player in mind to join the team: Angel Reese.
“If Rhy sends for you, you better get in the car and come,” Gray said. “When she sends for you in that car, you better get in that car because she ain’t circling the block for you again.”
The team pushed their chips all-in with the acquisition of Reese, trading multiple first-round picks for her.
She’s more than lived up to the expectations, breaking the single-season rebound record and single-game rebound record, while elevating her offense and defense.
This is where she wanted to be, too.
She wanted to be in Atlanta, but she wanted to be with Gray and Howard.

### Bring in the reinforcements
“They’re great vets,” Reese told The IX Sports. “Outside of the basketball stuff, they always are making sure that I’m good. Like they’re the first people to check on me with anything that’s going on. Basketball-wise, you don’t have to do it once the game is done, they don’t have to talk, because this is a business, honestly. But they genuinely care about me and the sisterhood in the locker room has been amazing. It’s something that I really needed, so I’m really grateful for them.”
And while they are teaching Reese how to win – she’ll be making her first playoff appearance in her three-year career with Atlanta – she’s teaching Gray how to be what she is off of the court.
A superstar.
“I was telling Lish that you’re a superstar, and she doesn’t realize that all the time. When we go places, they want to meet certain people,” Reese told The IX Sports. “She loves T.I., so I’m like, ‘You’re a superstar.’ Like, you go through the back entrance, you don’t go through the front.
“I’m trying to show her that you’re a star. All of those chants are for you, because you’re a superstar, and you belong here.”
It’s something that Gray has taken time to adjust to – even with that All-Star performance a couple of years ago.
“I guess it’s just like that humble nature of me. But yeah, Angel like she reiterates over and over that, ‘I _am_ Atlanta. There are no rules. We are Atlanta. We are superstars, and we need to start acting like it.’
“I’m like, you know what? Yeah, you’re right. I am a superstar. Like I do need to take advantage of my perks.”
That came to fruition during Atlanta’s Birthday Bash in May, when she got to see T.I. in concert.
When asked about her favorite song, Gray said, “Big Things Poppin’,” which was fitting for the play of the Dream this year.
Gray even got to meet The Rubber Band Man after the show.
A superstar, indeed.

### Quiet no longer
After each game, win or lose, the Dream huddle in front of their bench. Hillmon traditionally addressed the group first, serving as Atlanta’s vocal leader.
That’s not a role that Gray takes on, but that doesn’t mean that she is the quiet person that everyone thinks she is.
Take, for instance, an in-arena, mid-timeout video package that played in Gateway Center Arena.
Over the beat of Glorilla’s “WHATCHU KNO ABOUT ME,” Gray and Howard were rapping the lines to Dr. Suess’ Green Eggs and Ham over the beat.
Players like Jones, Paopao, and Indya Nivar had to cover their mouths to stifle their laughter.
It’s an example of the personality that sometimes shines through from Gray, despite the quiet, shy demeanor.
When asked about her quiet demeanor, Staley interrupted the question.
“She’s not quiet anymore,” she said, with a laugh. “She’s incredibly funny.”
And she’s not afraid to be the butt of the joke, either. During a video series called “Rewind the Tape,” I asked Gray to go over her high school scouting report.
In the report, it said that she had “springs in her legs” for her ability to jump.
She made a joke about needing some WD-40 for her knees now.
Likewise, during the team’s first preseason game, there was a Spanish player on the Dream’s training camp roster named Maite Cazorla.
During a pre-game media session, Gray was asked if she could speak Spanish or would learn how to from her teammate.
She said, “Me llamo Lish. Adios,” before ending the interview with a laugh.
Despite claiming that she doesn’t block shots, Gray blocks a fair number, especially for a guard.
But for her, she denies it and says, “That’s not me. That’s AI.”

### Big brand Lish
“I can’t tell you. I cannot tell you,” Wilson told The IX Sports in June when trying to get her to spill the news about a potential PE coming for her friend. “That’s her news to break for if she is, or if she’s not, but I can’t tell you that. But it’s definitely something special. And I always beam with so much more when she wears my shoes because she doesn’t have to, but she chooses to, and I’m glad that she likes it.”
It also doesn’t hurt that the league signed a new CBA, which allowed players to be paid fairly.
Last year, during the final season of the previous CBA, Gray made $190,000. After the new agreement was reached, when the overwhelming majority of players were free agents, Gray inked a new deal worth $1,190,000 in 2026 that increases over the next two seasons.
“It’s so crazy because like you’re young and you just remember like being in the backyard playing, and then you get to high school, and then you get to college, and then you get to the pros, and it’s just like I just sit back and I’ll be like, I be like, ‘wow, I made it,’” Gray reflected.
“Then, with the new CBA money, I’m like, ‘whoa, I really made it,’ because then it’s just like it allows me to throw a couple extra bucks to my parents and get them nice things that I wasn’t able to do in the past. So it’s just like I wake up looking at that bank account, and you know, just being able to realize that, wow. Like, I did it! I really made it!”
The added attention isn’t always positive attention. It’s been that way throughout the league over the last few years. With the added eyeballs comes the added trolls.
It isn’t new to Gray.
That mural in her hometown? It was vandalized in 2022 with racist comments written on it by three men.
“I just give my energy to the people who deserve it. I give my energy to people that also reciprocate that same energy back to me,” she said. “I’m not gonna waste my time on negative people and bad thoughts because that can take a toll on your mental health, as well.

### Big brand Lish
“So I think for me, I’m good at reading a person. Before I intrude on somebody or talk to them, I kind of like to sit back and study you and see how you move and how you talk to people. Are you nice? Are you respectful? And then from there, after my first conversation with you, I know that like, ‘OK, this is somebody that I can continue to talk to, or like, no, this is a one-time conversation for me, because for me, like I’ve always told, first impressions mean a lot. My spirit is too positive and fun to be wasted on negative people.”

## Still one goal to achieve
During the All-Star break this year, Gray joined her fellow All-Stars at the Barack Obama Presidential Center for a practice before the game.
The namesake came out and introduced himself to players and took photos – including with Gray.
Allisha Gray standing with Barack Obama (Photo credit: Allisha Gray on Threads)
Add that to the list of big-time moments for her to achieve this year, along with meeting T.I. and even having the rapper personalize a message for her during her Goggle Lish game.
“I was so happy. That made my night,” Gray told reporters after the game. “I took a picture with Obama, a picture with T.I, and got a personal message video from T.I. Year made.”
But there is one more thing that could make her year even better.
Despite all of the hardware. Despite being a multi-millionaire from playing the game that she has loved since she was playing in the backyard as a kid, Gray still has more to accomplish.
She didn’t say win the MVP, though she wouldn’t mind it.
She didn’t say lead the league in scoring (“the S in SG stands for shooting,” she said).
No.
The one goal that she wants to accomplish has nothing to do with her. It has to do with her team.
“The W Championship. That’s literally like the only thing from my career that is missing is a W Championship, and I feel like that’s something everybody wants to win,” Gray explained. “I really do feel like we have the team to accomplish that goal. We just gotta really lock in and stick to the game plan and really hone down on like the little minor mistakes that we tend to make. But I truly believe that we have the team to accomplish that goal this season.”
Even if that doesn’t happen this year, the team is confident in the players they have and the vision that they have for the future.
And that future, no matter what, includes Gray.
Something that her friends and family are proud of.
“With Lish, I think she’s happy in Atlanta. They allowed her to grow up,” Staley said. “She has a handful of friends who are super competitive and allowed her to grow. They are rising together at the top of their games.”

## Still one goal to achieve
“I’m glad that she’s seeing pieces surrounding her to be able to help her drive and continue to drive,” Wilson added. “But, I think she feels really good in Atlanta. I’m just glad that she’s found a home for herself. Because it shouldn’t be like, ‘no, I’m stable here,’ but it should be ‘I’m trying to make my footprint here.’ That’s what Lish is doing.”
And as far as her family goes, they couldn’t be happier to have her nearby.
“Having her come to Atlanta has been a blessing for us as a family, for her as a player,” Allen Gray said. “The class and the way that this organization is run is somewhere that she feels at home. She wants to end her career here because of the support and the wraparound services that they offer here in Atlanta. All of her needs are met, all of her requests are met, and the way that they take care of our daughter, we really appreciate it.”
So, all that leaves is Gray.
Just a kid from Sandersville. A quiet kid who loves the outdoors. Loves her family, her friends, her people.
She’s as close to her hometown as she can be, but in Atlanta, she _is_ home.
And that is where she wants to stay.
“I’m loved here in Atlanta. Atlanta has made me like this organization has made me feel so great about myself,” she said. “That’s why when it was time to extend and re-sign, there was no hesitation for me. This is a place I definitely want to retire and finish my career, playing for the Dream.
“It’s just the support here is so amazing. The little kids really like to make me feel good because no matter how I play, I can have an on night, off night; they don’t see that. All they see me as is Allisha the person, and they make me feel good regardless of the game that I have.”

The **2022–23 Tennessee Lady Volunteers basketball team** represented the University of Tennessee in the [2022–23](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_season "2022–23 NCAA Division I women's basketball season")college basketball season. Led by former Lady Vol Kellie Harper,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Tennessee_Lady_Volunteers_basketball_team#cite_note-1) entering her fourth year as head coach, the team played its games at Thompson–Boling Arena as members of the Southeastern Conference.

The Lady Vols finished the season with a 25–12 overall record, 13–3 in the conference. They advanced to the finals of the [SEC tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_SEC_women's_basketball_tournament "2023 SEC women's basketball tournament"), where they lost to South Carolina.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Tennessee_Lady_Volunteers_basketball_team#cite_note-2) Finishing strong in the conference, the Lady Vols earned an at-large bid to the [NCAA tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2023 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament"), advancing to the Sweet Sixteen before losing to Virginia Tech.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Tennessee_Lady_Volunteers_basketball_team#cite_note-3)
The 2021–22 team finished the season 25–9, 11–5 in third place in SEC play. They lost in the semifinals of the [SEC tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_SEC_women's_basketball_tournament "2022 SEC women's basketball tournament") to their rivals, Kentucky,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Tennessee_Lady_Volunteers_basketball_team#cite_note-4) who went on to win the tournament. The Lady Vols also received an at-large bid to the [NCAA tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2022 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament"), where they lost in the Sweet Sixteen to Louisville.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Tennessee_Lady_Volunteers_basketball_team#cite_note-5)

The **2022–23 Tennessee Lady Volunteers basketball team** represented the University of Tennessee in the [2022–23](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_season "2022–23 NCAA Division I women's basketball season")college basketball season. Led by former Lady Vol Kellie Harper,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Tennessee_Lady_Volunteers_basketball_team#cite_note-1) entering her fourth year as head coach, the team played its games at Thompson–Boling Arena as members of the Southeastern Conference.
texts.5:
The Lady Vols finished the season with a 25–12 overall record, 13–3 in the conference. They advanced to the finals of the [SEC tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_SEC_women's_basketball_tournament "2023 SEC women's basketball tournament"), where they lost to South Carolina.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Tennessee_Lady_Volunteers_basketball_team#cite_note-2) Finishing strong in the conference, the Lady Vols earned an at-large bid to the [NCAA tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2023 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament"), advancing to the Sweet Sixteen before losing to Virginia Tech.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Tennessee_Lady_Volunteers_basketball_team#cite_note-3)
The 2021–22 team finished the season 25–9, 11–5 in third place in SEC play. They lost in the semifinals of the [SEC tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_SEC_women's_basketball_tournament "2022 SEC women's basketball tournament") to their rivals, Kentucky,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Tennessee_Lady_Volunteers_basketball_team#cite_note-4) who went on to win the tournament. The Lady Vols also received an at-large bid to the [NCAA tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2022 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament"), where they lost in the Sweet Sixteen to Louisville.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Tennessee_Lady_Volunteers_basketball_team#cite_note-5)

The **2022–23 Clemson Tigers women's basketball team** represented Clemson University during the [2022–23](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_season "2022–23 NCAA Division I women's basketball season") college basketball season. The Tigers were led by fifth year head coach Amanda Butler. The Tigers, members of the Atlantic Coast Conference, played their home games at Littlejohn Coliseum.

The Tigers finished the season 19–16 and 7–11 in [ACC play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Atlantic_Coast_Conference_women's_basketball_season "2022–23 Atlantic Coast Conference women's basketball season") to finish in tenth place. As the tenth seed in the [ACC tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_ACC_women's_basketball_tournament "2023 ACC women's basketball tournament"), they defeated fifteenth seed [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Pittsburgh_Panthers_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 Pittsburgh Panthers women's basketball team") in the First Round before losing to seventh seed [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_North_Carolina_Tar_Heels_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 North Carolina Tar Heels women's basketball team") in the Second Round. They received an at-large invitation to the [WNIT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Women's_National_Invitation_Tournament "2023 Women's National Invitation Tournament"). The Tigers defeated [High Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Point_Panthers_women's_basketball "High Point Panthers women's basketball") in the First Round and [Auburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Auburn_Tigers_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 Auburn Tigers women's basketball team") in the Second Round before losing to [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Florida_Gators_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 Florida Gators women's basketball team") in the Super 16 to end their season.

The [Tigers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_Clemson_Tigers_women's_basketball_team "2021–22 Clemson Tigers women's basketball team") finished the season 10–21 and 3–15 in [ACC play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_Atlantic_Coast_Conference_women's_basketball_season "2021–22 Atlantic Coast Conference women's basketball season") to finish in thirteenth place. In the [ACC tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_ACC_women's_basketball_tournament "2022 ACC women's basketball tournament"), they defeated twelfth seeded [Syracuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_Syracuse_Orange_women's_basketball_team "2021–22 Syracuse Orange women's basketball team") in the First Round before losing to fifth seed [Virginia Tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_Virginia_Tech_Hokies_women's_basketball_team "2021–22 Virginia Tech Hokies women's basketball team") in the Second Round. They were not invited to the [NCAA tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2022 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament") or the [WNIT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Women's_National_Invitation_Tournament "2022 Women's National Invitation Tournament").

texts.5: The **2022–23 Clemson Tigers women's basketball team** represented Clemson University during the [2022–23](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_season "2022–23 NCAA Division I women's basketball season") college basketball season. The Tigers were led by fifth year head coach Amanda Butler. The Tigers, members of the Atlantic Coast Conference, played their home games at Littlejohn Coliseum.
texts.6: The Tigers finished the season 19–16 and 7–11 in [ACC play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Atlantic_Coast_Conference_women's_basketball_season "2022–23 Atlantic Coast Conference women's basketball season") to finish in tenth place. As the tenth seed in the [ACC tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_ACC_women's_basketball_tournament "2023 ACC women's basketball tournament"), they defeated fifteenth seed [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Pittsburgh_Panthers_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 Pittsburgh Panthers women's basketball team") in the First Round before losing to seventh seed [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_North_Carolina_Tar_Heels_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 North Carolina Tar Heels women's basketball team") in the Second Round. They received an at-large invitation to the [WNIT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Women's_National_Invitation_Tournament "2023 Women's National Invitation Tournament"). The Tigers defeated [High Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Point_Panthers_women's_basketball "High Point Panthers women's basketball") in the First Round and [Auburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Auburn_Tigers_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 Auburn Tigers women's basketball team") in the Second Round before losing to [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Florida_Gators_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 Florida Gators women's basketball team") in the Super 16 to end their season.
texts.7:
The [Tigers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_Clemson_Tigers_women's_basketball_team "2021–22 Clemson Tigers women's basketball team") finished the season 10–21 and 3–15 in [ACC play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_Atlantic_Coast_Conference_women's_basketball_season "2021–22 Atlantic Coast Conference women's basketball season") to finish in thirteenth place. In the [ACC tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_ACC_women's_basketball_tournament "2022 ACC women's basketball tournament"), they defeated twelfth seeded [Syracuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_Syracuse_Orange_women's_basketball_team "2021–22 Syracuse Orange women's basketball team") in the First Round before losing to fifth seed [Virginia Tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_Virginia_Tech_Hokies_women's_basketball_team "2021–22 Virginia Tech Hokies women's basketball team") in the Second Round. They were not invited to the [NCAA tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2022 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament") or the [WNIT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Women's_National_Invitation_Tournament "2022 Women's National Invitation Tournament").

The **2022–23 Clemson Tigers women's basketball team** represented Clemson University during the [2022–23](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_season "2022–23 NCAA Division I women's basketball season") college basketball season. The Tigers were led by fifth year head coach Amanda Butler. The Tigers, members of the Atlantic Coast Conference, played their home games at Littlejohn Coliseum.

The Tigers finished the season 19–16 and 7–11 in [ACC play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Atlantic_Coast_Conference_women's_basketball_season "2022–23 Atlantic Coast Conference women's basketball season") to finish in tenth place. As the tenth seed in the [ACC tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_ACC_women's_basketball_tournament "2023 ACC women's basketball tournament"), they defeated fifteenth seed [Pittsburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Pittsburgh_Panthers_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 Pittsburgh Panthers women's basketball team") in the First Round before losing to seventh seed [North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_North_Carolina_Tar_Heels_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 North Carolina Tar Heels women's basketball team") in the Second Round. They received an at-large invitation to the [WNIT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Women's_National_Invitation_Tournament "2023 Women's National Invitation Tournament"). The Tigers defeated [High Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High_Point_Panthers_women's_basketball "High Point Panthers women's basketball") in the First Round and [Auburn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Auburn_Tigers_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 Auburn Tigers women's basketball team") in the Second Round before losing to [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022%E2%80%9323_Florida_Gators_women's_basketball_team "2022–23 Florida Gators women's basketball team") in the Super 16 to end their season.

The [Tigers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_Clemson_Tigers_women's_basketball_team "2021–22 Clemson Tigers women's basketball team") finished the season 10–21 and 3–15 in [ACC play](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_Atlantic_Coast_Conference_women's_basketball_season "2021–22 Atlantic Coast Conference women's basketball season") to finish in thirteenth place. In the [ACC tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_ACC_women's_basketball_tournament "2022 ACC women's basketball tournament"), they defeated twelfth seeded [Syracuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_Syracuse_Orange_women's_basketball_team "2021–22 Syracuse Orange women's basketball team") in the First Round before losing to fifth seed [Virginia Tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_Virginia_Tech_Hokies_women's_basketball_team "2021–22 Virginia Tech Hokies women's basketball team") in the Second Round. They were not invited to the [NCAA tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_NCAA_Division_I_women's_basketball_tournament "2022 NCAA Division I women's basketball tournament") or the [WNIT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Women's_National_Invitation_Tournament "2022 Women's National Invitation Tournament").

**FINAL WRAP**

Selected to the prestigious WBCA All-America Team in both 2013 and 2014, Dolson was an Associated Press Second Team All-American and USBWA All-America pick during her senior campaign ... Also selected as the Senior CLASS Award winner and American Athletic Conference Defensive Player of the Year in 2013-14 ... Tied for second all-time at UConn with 154 games played and is the all-time leader with 152 starts ... Finished her career 12th on UConn's all-time scoring list at 1,797 career points, fourth with 1,101 career rebounds and fourth in both blocks (254) and field goal percentage (58.8 percent) ... A member of the All-Conference Tournament Team in all four years at UConn, Dolson also earned a spot on the All-NCAA Tournament Team in 2014 and on the NCAA Tournament All-Regional Team in both 2012 and 2014 ... A two-time All-Conference First Team selection, the Port Jervis, N.Y. native has notched one of only three triple-doubles in school history ... One of only four Huskies, along with Tina Charles, Rebecca Lobo and Jamelle Elliott, with at least 1,000 points and 1,000 rebounds.
**2013-14 SEASON**

Started in all 40 of UConn's game, averaging 12.5 points and a team-best 9.3 rebounds per contest ... Shot 56.4 percent from the floor and was fourth on the team at 3.4 assists per game ... Hauled in 371 rebounds, which was one shy of tying UConn's single-season record held by Tina Charles ... Blocked 93 shots, which was the third-highest total by a Husky senior ... Notched what was then only the second triple-double in school history with a 26-point, 14-rebound, 11-assists performance in the win over Oregon (Nov. 20) ... Pulled down a season-high 16 rebounds in the national championship game victory over Notre Dame (April 8). Dolson also recorded 17 points and dished-out seven assists in her final collegiate game ... Averaged 11.7 points and 10.3 rebounds per game while shooting 51.6 percent en route to being honored on the All-Conference Tournament Team for the fourth-straight year ... Averaged 13.0 points, 9.0 rebounds and shot 57.9 percent from the floor during UConn's six-game run through the NCAA Tournament.
**2012-13 SEASON:**

Played and started in 38 of UConn's 39 games and was third on the team with 13.6 points while leading the squad with 7.1 rebounds per game ... Third on the team at 26.8 minutes per game and led the squad with a solid .598 field goal percentage, which was the second-highest total nationally ... Became a legitimate 3-point shooting threat during her junior season, connecting on 8-19 attempts from long range after entering the year 0-3 from deep ... Put together another solid year from the charity stripe, connecting on .796 percent (82-103) of her free throws ... One of three Huskies to dish at least 100 assists, Dolson was third with 117 helpers. Also boasted a 1.36 assist/turnover ratio in 2012-13 after entering the year with a career A/TO ratio of 0.74 ... Scored in double-figures 31 times and totaled at least 20 points on six occasions ... Posted four double-double performances after entering the year with only two to her credit ... Led the team in scoring nine times and led the squad in rebounds on 12 occasions ... Posted a career-high 25 points twice, the first time in UConn's 87-62 win over Syracuse (Jan. 19) and then again in the 85-51 victory over USF (March 2). Dolson was 8-11 from the field, 9-9 from the free throw line and also grabbed 10 rebounds against the Bulls ... Played her way onto her third-straight All-BIG EAST Tournament team with an 18-point, 14-rebound effort in the 61-59 loss to Notre Dame in the BIG EAST Championship Final (March 4) ... Suffered through a couple injuries towards the end of the season but still managed to average 11.2 points and lead the squad with 8.2 rebounds per game during the postseason. Also shot .581 percent from the field and .824 from the free throw line in the Huskies' nine postseason contests.
**2011-12 SEASON**

Led the Huskies in rebounding in the 2011-12 campaign pulling down 6.0 grabs per game and was the leader in blocks with 57 denials... Dolson tallied 20 double-figure performances, including four 20-plus games... Dolson opened up the season with a bang going 6-for-6 from the floor for 12 points and added seven rebounds against Holy Cross (Nov. 13)... Stefanie had nine points, nine rebounds and a season-high four blocks... On Nov. 26 Dolson registered 17 points and was perfect from the charity stripe (3-for-3)... Had 11 points and seven rebounds in only 13 minutes of action against Dayton (Nov. 27)... Dolson was a rebound shy of a double-double versus Texas A&M (Dec. 6) when she scored 10 points and brought in nine boards... She set a new career-high with 11 made field goals en route to 22 points against Fairfield (Dec. 29)...Dolson led the team with seven grabs and six assists versus West Virginia (Jan. 4)... Stefanie had a team-high 10 rebounds along with nine points at Notre Dame (Jan. 7)... Against USF (Jan. 28) Dolson recorded her first double-double of the 2012 season with 22 points and 18 rebounds and added three blocks on the night... She was perfect at Duke (Jan. 30) as she went 4-for-4 from the field and 2-for-2 from the foul line for 10 points... Led the team in scoring with 16 points in only 20 minutes of action against Rutgers (Feb. 4)... Netted 18 points and seven grabs versus Notre Dame (Feb. 27)...
